items.title: Rethinking Health Care Regulatory Sandboxes Under the European Union AI Act
items.abstract: Abstract AI models have enabled substantial advances in health care. Since the entry into force of the European Union (EU) AI Act in 2024, these systems have become subject to a common regulatory framework in the EU intended to harmonize AI governance across all member states. One of the act’s distinctive features is that it accommodates existing economic, technological, and regulatory differences among European countries by leaving certain implementation responsibilities to national authorities. This is evident in regulatory sandboxes, supervised environments for developing, testing, and validating AI systems before deployment. In this viewpoint, we provide a policy-oriented analysis of health care regulatory sandboxes under the EU AI Act and propose recommendations for their design. These recommendations address the need to document model compression techniques that may affect the classification of large high-risk systems above the 10 25 floating point operations per second threshold, incorporate explainability into AI systems from the design stage, identify and document biases in health care datasets, clarify the treatment of federated learning parameter updates under the General Data Protection Regulation, and strengthen the oversight of AI agents in clinical environments. The implementation timeline makes this discussion particularly timely given the approaching deadline of August 2, 2027, by which all member states must have established at least one national regulatory sandbox.

items.title: RUGON: A Community-Based Earthquake Observation and Rapid Response Platform for Thailand
items.abstract: Abstract The 28 March 2025 Mw 7.7 Myanmar earthquake showed that a large regional earthquake can produce extensive ground shaking throughout Thailand even though it occurred 1000 km away. This earthquake caused prolonged shaking of high-rise buildings and disruption of activities in major cities, emphasizing the need for rapid earthquake information to support community response. Although Thailand maintains national seismic monitoring networks, there has been no operational earthquake early warning (EEW) available to the public. This article presents RUGON (Real-time Ubiquitous Ground-shaking Observation Network), a community-based earthquake observation and rapid response platform designed to deliver timely ground-motion information by integrating distributed microelectromechanical systems accelerometers, edge computing, cloud processing, and web-based decision-support tools. The platform supports community notification, structural vibration monitoring, and real-time situational awareness during earthquake emergencies. Analysis of strong-motion records from the 28 March 2025 Myanmar earthquake shows that, if rapid detection and communication are implemented, a regional earthquake may provide more than one minute of available lead time for major Thai cities. Sensor performance was verified through laboratory calibration against laser Doppler vibrometer measurements. Field deployment during the 18 May 2026 ML 5.3 Myanmar earthquake successfully demonstrated the complete RUGON workflow, from sensing and communication to notification and visualization, under real earthquake conditions. RUGON is a rapid earthquake information and situational-awareness platform that reports observed ground motion in near-real time for rapid alert and response. It is not a substitute for a national EEW system. Nevertheless, because regional earthquakes affecting Thailand originate from distant sources, even peak-ground-acceleration-based observations without P-wave prediction still provide a usable interval for alert and response. Community-scale observations of strong shaking upstream can provide actionable information before it reaches distant communities.

items.title: Rural Movements and Parliaments in Europe as Agents of Socio-Political Landscapes: Social Innovation, Identity Re-Creation, Democratic Renewal and Professionalisation in Times of Rural Transformation
items.abstract: European rural communities face profound transformations driven by demographic change, economic restructuring, service erosion, and political marginalisation. In response, Rural Movements (RMs) and Rural Parliaments (RPs) have emerged as important actors shaping the socio-political dimensions of rural landscapes. Drawing on the European Landscape Convention’s understanding of landscape as shaped by both natural and human factors, this article conceptualises RMs and RPs as co-producers of rural socio-political landscapes through advocacy, identity-building, community mobilisation, and institutional engagement. The study combines a qualitative literature review with exploratory empirical material from two expert workshops conducted at the 6th European Rural Parliament (Inverurie, Scotland, October 2025), involving representatives from eight European countries. The analysis examines RMs and RPs as agents of social innovation, arenas of identity preservation and reinvention, infrastructures of democratic renewal, and navigators of the professionalisation-institutionalisation dilemma. Findings suggest that many movements emerged in response to centralisation, service loss, weakened local influence, and democratic deficits. Professionalisation is understood as the development of organisational capacities, advocacy skills, and strategic networks while maintaining grassroots legitimacy and local embeddedness. The article identifies key factors that enable and constrain movement development and concludes that the transformative potential of RMs and RPs depends on balancing organisational effectiveness with participatory, locally rooted, and politically autonomous forms of action.

items.title: Safety, accuracy, empathy and information quality of six large language models answering patient-facing questions about diabetic kidney disease: a cross-sectional comparative study
items.abstract: Background Large language models (LLMs) may support patient education, but their suitability for diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains uncertain. We compared six publicly accessible LLM chatbots—ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, Doubao, Kimi, and Qwen—across safety, accuracy, empathy, information quality, and readability, with safety as the primary outcome. Methods In this CHART-guided cross-sectional study, 42 standardized English DKD questions were submitted once to each chatbot in independent single-turn sessions, generating 252 responses. Five source-masked clinical raters assessed safety, accuracy, empathy, DISCERN, EQIP, JAMA benchmarks, and the Global Quality Scale; readability was assessed automatically. Agreement was evaluated using Fleiss' κ and ICC (2,1)/ICC (2,5). Model differences were tested using Cochran's Q or Friedman tests with Kendall's W and Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Potentially unsafe responses underwent qualitative review. Results Safety showed substantial agreement ( κ = 0.854); ICC (2,1) ranged from 0.552 to 0.855 and ICC (2,5) from 0.860 to 0.967. Safe-response rates ranged from 83.3% to 92.9% without significant between-model differences ( P = 0.726). Accuracy and empathy differed significantly (both P < 0.001), with ChatGPT highest for accuracy and Gemini highest for clinician-rated empathy. Information quality also differed significantly, with ChatGPT performing best overall and Doubao lowest. All six readability indices differed across models (all P < 0.001; Kendall's W = 0.139–0.255). DeepSeek had the lowest mean scores on all five grade-level indices and the highest mean FRES, but mean grade-level estimates exceeded the sixth-grade reference level for every model. Thirty of 252 responses (11.9%) were potentially unsafe, most often because of incomplete medication-related information or insufficiently individualized fluid advice. Conclusions Publicly accessible LLMs can provide plausible DKD information but show variable performance and safety risks. They may support, but should not replace, professional patient education; guideline anchoring, source verification, improved readability, and clinical oversight remain essential.

items.title: Schur complements of sectorial matrices: proof corrections and a sharp mean inequality
items.abstract: This technical note examines proof steps in ‘The Schur complement inequalities involving sectorial matrices’ by Marziyeh Irandegani, Mojtaba Bakherad and Monire Hajmohamadi (Linear and Multilinear Algebra, 2026; DOI: 10.1080/03081087.2026.2751934). An exact positive-definite 2×2 example disproves the interchange of a Schur complement with an integral used in the proofs of Theorems 2.2, 2.6 and 2.9. A separate sectorial example disproves an intermediate norm comparison in the proof of Proposition 3.1. These examples do not disprove the stated main inequalities. A self-contained corrected argument establishes the sharp factor sec²(α) for the matrix-mean inequality and the normalized operator-monotone functional inequality, improving the factors sec⁴(α) stated in the reviewed article. Sharpness is established for every fixed positive block size. A unitarily invariant norm consequence has factor sec³(α), improving sec⁵(α); optimality of the norm factor is not claimed. The final conclusion of the reviewed Proposition 3.1 is explicitly left unresolved. No exhaustive literature-priority claim is made. Files: the technical note in PDF and a ZIP package containing the PDF, editable LaTeX source, README and a Python script using exact rational arithmetic to verify the displayed examples. The reviewed publisher PDF is not redistributed. items.title: Self Learning AI and Big Data for Resilient Cybersecurity in Distributed Networks
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of large scale computer networks driven by cloud infrastructures, Internet of Things environments, and distributed digital services has significantly increased the complexity of cybersecurity threats. Traditional rule based security systems often struggle to detect evolving and previously unseen attacks within high volume network traffic. This study proposes a self learning artificial intelligence approach designed to enhance threat detection capability in large scale computer networks by leveraging adaptive learning mechanisms and large scale network data analysis. The proposed framework integrates machine learning models with big data processing techniques to continuously learn from network traffic patterns, behavioral anomalies, and historical security events. Through automated feature extraction and iterative model refinement, the system dynamically improves its ability to identify malicious activities without relying solely on predefined signatures. This study adopts a qualitative conceptual evaluation approach to examine the proposed self-learning artificial intelligence and big data framework for cybersecurity resilience in distributed computer networks. The evaluation is conducted through literature synthesis, comparative analysis of existing intrusion detection approaches, architectural modeling, and conceptual validation of the proposed framework against key cybersecurity requirements, including adaptability, scalability, continuous learning, and detection coverage for known and unknown threats. The system also shows strong scalability in processing high volume network data while maintaining stable detection performance. These results indicate that integrating self learning artificial intelligence with scalable data processing can strengthen cybersecurity resilience in large scale computer networks and support the development of more adaptive and intelligent network defense mechanisms for future digital infrastructures.

items.title: Self Learning Artificial Intelligence for Autonomous Threat Detection in Computer Networks
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of large-scale computer networks and the exponential growth of big data have significantly increased the complexity and frequency of cyber threats, rendering traditional signature-based security mechanisms inadequate for adaptive detection. This study aims to develop a self-learning AI model capable of autonomously identifying evolving attack patterns and anomalous behaviors in large-scale networks without relying exclusively on pre-labeled datasets. The proposed framework integrates deep neural architectures, incremental learning, and behavior-based traffic analysis to enable continuous adaptation to dynamic threat environments while ensuring computational efficiency and scalability. The model was trained and evaluated using realistic network traffic datasets simulating distributed attacks, zero-day exploits, and advanced persistent threats across heterogeneous environments. Experimental findings demonstrate that the self-learning approach enhances detection accuracy, reduces false positives, and accelerates response times compared to conventional intrusion detection systems. In addition, the combination of deep neural architectures with incremental learning and scalable data processing further strengthens model robustness and adaptability in complex and evolving networks. The results indicate that integrating adaptive AI into cybersecurity frameworks enhances proactive defense capabilities, improves resilience in large-scale computer networks, and provides a scalable, intelligent solution for next-generation threat detection systems. This study highlights the practical relevance of combining AI, big data analytics, and cybersecurity strategies to support intelligent, adaptive security solutions capable of addressing emerging threats, minimizing operational risks, and fostering robust network protection in increasingly complex digital infrastructures.

items.title: Seven Human Qualities for the New Era: Leadership Beyond Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Written companion to the guest lecture "Seven Human Qualities for the New Era: Leadership Beyond Artificial Intelligence", delivered by Prof. Dr. Stoyana Natseva as a pre-recorded lecture at the international webinar "Your Future Starts Now: Leadership and Innovation for Finance and Business", organised by Kimyo International University in Tashkent (KIUT), Uzbekistan, on 14 October 2026. The paper is not a transcript; it sets out the argument of the lecture in academic form. Starting from the observation that people often know what they should do and still find it difficult to do it, the paper proposes seven human qualities that may matter more as artificial intelligence makes information widely available: emotional maturity, adaptability, the ability to learn, critical thinking, responsibility, resilience, and the ability to communicate and work with people. Each quality is related to established research and to its implications for finance and business education. The seven qualities are presented as a teaching framework for discussion, not as a validated competency model. This version has not undergone peer review.

items.title: SHAPING PUBLIC EMPLOYEES’ AI PERCEPTIONS: THE ROLES OF DIGITAL LEADERSHIP AND INNOVATION CLIMATE
items.abstract: This study examines how digital leadership shapes public employees’ perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), with innovation climate modeled as a mediating mechanism under Social Learning Theory. Survey data from 314 public employees in southern Türkiye were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Results indicate that digital leadership positively predicts both innovation climate and AI perceptions, and that innovation climate itself enhances AI perceptions. Mediation analysis shows a partial indirect effect of digital leadership on AI perceptions through innovation climate. The study links leadership and organizational climate perspectives to explain technology-related perceptions in the public sector and suggests that strengthening digital leadership capabilities and cultivating an innovation-oriented climate are critical for effective and sustainable AI adoption in public administration.

items.abstract: Synergy of Human Capital 5.0 and Artificial Intelligence in Business Decision-Making to Enhance MSME Competitiveness in the Digital Economy Era. The digital economy and the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are changing how micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) make decisions and which skills they need. However, AI adoption does not automatically improve competitiveness because it depends on the readiness of people and management. This article aims to (1) analyze how AI disruption and automation reshape competence requirements in MSMEs, (2) examine the role of Human Capital 5.0 in using AI for business decisions, (3) identify opportunities, challenges, and the roles of management and education in human–AI synergy, and (4) formulate a conceptual framework of that synergy. The study is a structured qualitative literature review of 29 sources published in 2022–2026, consisting of international and national journal articles, the author’s earlier studies, and reports from international and government institutions, analyzed through thematic synthesis. The review shows that the literature mostly addresses AI adoption from technological and organizational angles, while human competence as a determinant of decision quality has not been fully integrated. Human Capital 5.0 functions as the ability to interpret, test, and control AI outputs, whereas AI extends data-processing and prediction capacity. Management shapes this synergy through leadership, human resource development, and responsible AI governance, while education supplies competencies and collaboration with MSMEs. The article proposes a five-stage conceptual model supported by leadership, digital readiness, data quality, technology access, and ethics, together with four propositions for future empirical testing. The model remains propositional and requires empirical validation. Strengthening MSMEs therefore requires combining AI literacy training, mentoring, cross-sector collaboration, and responsible AI governance.

items.title: Slippery or Safe Runways? Evaluating the New ICAO Runway Surface Condition Reporting Methodology
items.abstract: Runway surface conditions, particularly in cold and icy environments, pose a significant challenge to aircraft operations. To enhance safety and standardisation, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) adopted the Global Reporting Format (GRF) in 2016 and made it applicable from 4 November 2021, replacing previous assessment methods, including SNOWTAM reports and braking action conditions. This study evaluates how the implementation of the GRF has been perceived and experienced by two key aviation stakeholder groups, airport operators and flight crews; it does not measure the technical accuracy or the safety performance of the GRF directly. It also includes a comprehensive literature review on the evolution of runway condition reporting since 1956. The research combines a questionnaire survey of 112 pilots, recruited mainly through Central and Northern European airlines and pilot associations, with written open-ended questionnaires completed by nine airport operators in Slovakia and the Czech Republic. While pilots largely appreciate the improved clarity and structure of the updated SNOWTAM format, concerns remain over the removal of braking action assessments, which previously aided aircraft performance calculations and improved the situational awareness. Additionally, the study highlights inconsistencies across different airports, particularly in the measurement of runway contaminants. Airport operators have expressed concerns about the subjectivity of visual assessments, the absence of standardised measurement techniques, and the limitations of the Runway Condition Assessment Matrix (RCAM), which does not account for different runway surfaces. In the perception of the respondents, the GRF has improved the standardisation and clarity of runway condition reporting, whereas its effects on airport workload and operational safety are viewed with considerably more reservation. Given the regional scope of the samples and the absence of objective braking-performance or safety-outcome data, these results represent stakeholder-based evidence and identify potential concerns that require further validation. The respondents’ feedback suggests that further refinements may be needed to enhance consistency and reliability. The study proposes measures to address current limitations, including improved contaminant measurement techniques and a reassessment of the methodology to incorporate variations in runway surface properties. These insights contribute to the ongoing discourse on aviation safety and provide recommendations for optimising runway surface condition reporting, particularly in cold weather environments.

items.title: Smart surveillance for smart cities: methods, operational considerations, and emerging technologies for urban dengue vector surveillance in Southeast Asia
items.abstract: Rapid urbanization in Southeast Asia has created complex, heterogeneous landscapes that facilitate the proliferation of Aedes mosquitoes, the primary vectors of dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and other arboviruses. Megacities present particular surveillance challenges because vector populations vary across neighborhoods, building types, microhabitats, and vertical levels, while conventional indices may provide incomplete information on adult abundance and transmission risk. This narrative review synthesizes conventional and emerging approaches for monitoring immature and adult Aedes mosquitoes in urban environments, with emphasis on how surveillance tools can be combined to answer operational public-health questions. We examine the strengths, limitations, operational requirements, and urban applicability of larval surveys, ovitraps, adult traps, automated monitoring, molecular approaches, remote sensing, community-based surveillance, and artificial-intelligence-enabled systems. Rather than treating individual tools as interchangeable, we consider surveillance design across horizontal and vertical urban strata and discuss how sampling intensity can be adapted to local heterogeneity, resource availability, and the decision that surveillance is intended to support. We further examine how entomological observations can be integrated with epidemiological data, weather, land use, urban morphology, and human mobility to identify areas requiring intensified investigation or control. The review proposes a decision-oriented and tiered framework in which low-cost or automated sentinel surveillance provides continuous situational awareness, while targeted field investigation is triggered by entomological, environmental, epidemiological, or model-based signals. This perspective provides practical guidance for developing scalable, context-appropriate surveillance systems for rapidly urbanizing Southeast Asian cities.

items.title: SOCA: A Conversational Agent for Facility Location Problems
items.abstract: Facility location problems (FLPs) underpin decisions in emergency response, healthcare access, and infrastructure siting, yet applying them requires both optimization modeling skills and substantial spatial data preparation. This paper presents SOCA (Spatial Optimization Conversational Agent), a system that confines a large language model (LLM) to classifying the formulation and extracting scalar parameters through schema-validated function calls and delegates study area resolution, open-data acquisition, distance computation, and exact solution of four classic FLP formulations (P-Median, P-Center, MCLP, and LSCP) to deterministic tools. Every specification is confirmed by the user before solving, and solutions can be reported with substitutability and spatial equity diagnostics. We present SOCA as a technical feasibility study. Worked examples show how requests become staged, user-confirmed specifications; the MILP encodings reproduce the optima of a reference implementation exactly; and the data pipeline returned the targeted input layers across seven study areas, including cities in Africa and South Asia, using primary or fallback sources; retrieval does not establish data quality. A Manhattan fire station case illustrates coverage trade-offs and post-solve diagnostics on road network distances. Measuring interpretation accuracy, comparison against other LLM tool workflows, and a usability study with non-technical users remain future work.

items.title: Social Factors in Setting Up a New Works
items.abstract: This chapter examines the social and organizational challenges involved in setting up a new industrial works, drawing on Eric J. Miller’s analysis of the Spencer Works steel plant developed by Richard Thomas & Baldwins. Miller argues that technological development routinely outpaces the evolution of social institutions, leading to underutilization of human capacity, organizational conflict, and performance gaps. Addressing these issues requires treating organization building as a central task rather than a secondary consequence of plant design. Using a socio-technical systems framework, the chapter distinguishes four interdependent tasks in establishing a new works: plant design, plant construction, organization design, and organization building. Miller demonstrates that these processes form a single system of activities whose coordination is critical to the effectiveness of the final operating organization. The Spencer Works case illustrates the risks of separating technical and organizational planning, particularly when conventional management assumptions constrain innovation in work design and authority relations. Miller highlights the paradox of expecting a future operating organization to design itself while simultaneously being shaped by inherited structures and time pressures. Subsequent integration of plant and organizational design under operational leadership allowed some anticipatory accommodation between social and technical demands, though financial, temporal, and technological constraints limited its scope. The chapter concludes that while socio-technical analysis cannot eliminate uncertainty in green-field developments, it provides a disciplined way of anticipating tensions, managing human factors, and supporting more adaptive and effective organizational formation.

items.title: Social robotics for inclusive socio-emotional learning
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed educational research, creating new opportunities for designing inclusive, personalized, and learner-centred educational environments. Among emerging technologies, social robotics has gained increasing attention for its potential to support the cognitive, communicative, and socio-emotional development of learners with diverse educational needs. Unlike conventional educational technologies, social robots interact naturally through speech, gestures, facial expressions, eye contact, and emotional feedback, fostering communication and active engagement (Pennazio, 2017). Digital innovation has become a strategic resource for promoting educational quality and inclusion. As Calvani (2013) argues, technology should not be viewed as an educational goal but as a pedagogical tool capable of improving learning when integrated into evidence-based teaching practices. Within this perspective, social robotics combines artificial intelligence with inclusive pedagogy, promoting participation, individualized instruction, and socio-emotional development. items.title: Societal Impact of Deepfakes
items.abstract: Deepfake technology, which is synthetic audiovisual media developed using deep learning architecture (including Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and diffusion models), has transitioned from technical novelty to one of the most important sociotechnical developments of the early 21st century. The impact of deepfakes on society is explored in this chapter in terms of cybersecurity, education, and training; digital humans; digital immortality; media literacy; and adolescent mental health. Using peer-reviewed articles, court documents, government research initiatives, and data from industry, published between 2019 and 2025, as its sources, this chapter concludes that deepfakes are neither inherently harmful nor definitively helpful. Instead, they are amplifiers of existing social conditions, reflecting both the opportunity for harm and the opportunity for benefit. This chapter connects deepfake phenomena to the neuroscientific constructs of perception articulated by Roswandowitz and colleagues at the University of Zurich, analyzes the degree to which adolescent brain development renders adolescents especially susceptible to abuse of synthetic media, and discusses real examples of deepfake abuse in Hong Kong, Argentina, the Philippines, India, Spain, and South Korea. This chapter closes with a responsible governance framework consisting of origin infrastructure, tiered legal structures, universal media literacy, and victim services.

items.title: STLC Manager: Benchmarking LLM-Driven Model-to-Test Transformation and Test Case Optimization
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate software tests from heterogeneous artifacts, but semantic redundancy and stochastic output variability complicate reliable pre-execution refinement. This paper presents STLC Manager, an LLM-supported framework that transforms requirements, UML/XML models, and source code into structured test scenarios and test cases and supports Serial, Bulk, and Parallel strategies for semantic redundancy reduction. Validation combines archived cross-model evidence with a controlled local study of 60 runs over two fixed 64-case suites, three installed models, partitioned local Bulk and Controlled Local Parallel, and five repetitions per configuration. The evaluation also reconstructs a three-rater human consensus and includes a deterministic TF–IDF reference. In the controlled study, mean Test Redundancy Ratio ranged from 0.0063 to 0.5000 for partitioned Bulk and from 0.1250 to 0.6375 for Parallel. Item-level modal agreement ranged from 98.44% to 100% for Bulk and from 75.31% to 97.19% for Parallel, while mean artifact-scoped Scenario Coverage Preservation ranged from 0.900 to 1.000. The results show greater configuration sensitivity for Parallel under the evaluated protocol. However, the workloads differ and do not support a causal ranking of the strategies. The implementation is publicly available. The conclusions are limited to pre-execution semantic refinement and do not establish executability, coverage, mutation adequacy, or fault detection.

items.title: Strategi Kepala Sekolah dalam Membangun Budaya Mutu Berbasis Nilai Amanah dan Ihsan: Perspektif Total Quality Management dalam Transformasi Akreditasi C ke A
items.abstract: School accreditation in Indonesia is often reduced to completing documents before the assessment visit, so the quality it produces tends to be administrative and short-lived. SDIT Ar Refah Tanjungpinang faced the same problem before it raised its accreditation rating from C to A. This study aims to analyse the principal's strategies for building a quality culture from a Total Quality Management perspective, to explain how the values of amanah (trustworthiness) and ihsan (excellence) are internalised into that culture, and to reveal the impact of this culture on the accreditation transformation. The study employed a qualitative approach with a single case study design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and document analysis involving the principal, teachers, administrative staff, foundation board members, the school committee, and the accreditation team. The data were analysed using the interactive model of data condensation, data display, and conclusion drawing, and their trustworthiness was tested through source and technique triangulation. The findings show that the principal built a quality culture through shared quality awareness, documented work cycles, improvement-oriented evaluation, team collaboration, and role modelling. Amanah and ihsan served as intrinsic motivation that shifted work orientation from compliance to worship. The study concludes that integrating TQM principles with amanah and ihsan produces a substantive accreditation transformation, because quality is embraced as a moral and spiritual responsibility of the entire school community.

items.title: Student Interpretation and Negotiation of AI-Generated Critique in Design Studio Education: A Feedback Literacy and Cooperative Learning Perspective
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in design education, where it can provide students with fast, repeated suggestions or critiques on their work. This study examines how design students interpret AI-generated critique individually and how they negotiate its relevance with their group when making studio design decisions. Feedback literacy and two cooperative learning processes serve as the analytical lenses. The study is a cross-sectional, convergent mixed-methods survey of 77 visual communication design students in a studio course. This article reports a post hoc, theory-guided secondary analysis of three composites, together with five open-ended questions. Perceptions of AI as a reflective partner were positively associated with both group processing and reflection and promotive interaction, and both associations remained significant after Holm correction. After removing items whose wording referred to both AI and group work, the associations were smaller but still positive (? = .545 and .421) and are taken as the conservative basis for interpretation. Students who viewed AI more favorably as a reflective partner also reported greater team reflection and mutual support. Reflexive thematic analysis of the open-ended responses from all 77 respondents produced four themes: reflective noticing prompted by AI critique, appraising and selectively using AI suggestions, negotiating AI suggestions through group discussion, and positioning AI as support while retaining human judgment.

items.title: Student motivation and social loafing in shared-graded group work: the roles of cultural values and performance
items.abstract: Students respond differently to shared-graded group projects in higher education. This study examined how students’ individualism, collectivism, and academic performance relate to intrinsic motivation, externally regulated motivation, social loafing, and satisfaction with the group. A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 292 university students in Norway and Bangladesh. Measurement invariance and multigroup structural tests supported pooling the country samples for the parallel-mediation model. Collectivism and academic performance were associated with higher levels of both intrinsic and externally regulated motivation, together with lower social loafing. Individualism showed a different pattern, with lower intrinsic motivation and higher social loafing, but also higher externally regulated motivation. Satisfaction was positively associated with both motivation forms and negatively with social loafing. Collectivism and academic performance had positive indirect associations with satisfaction, whereas individualism’s total indirect association was nonsignificant. The findings suggest that caring about the shared grade does not necessarily imply intrinsic interest or lower loafing.

items.title: Synthetic Sincerity
items.abstract: Isaacs, M. (Director). (2025). Synthetic Sincerity. Icarus Films. 70 mins. Synthetic Sincerity is a film that encapsulates so much of the reality of what it means to be a filmmaker in the age of AI and exemplifies Werner Herzog’s ecstatic truth where facts take a back seat to exploring a deeper truth by utilizing fiction in documentary to engage an audience with authenticity (whatever that may mean). Herzog famously quotes André Gide, “I modify facts to such a degree that they resemble truth more than reality,” a quote that has not been attributed to Gide outside of Herzog’s quoting it in numerous interviews. Similarly, filmmaker Marc Isaacs and writer Adam Ganz invite the audience into a world that without context and upon first viewing appears to be somewhat of a traditional documentary, only to reveal in the final scenes that all may not have been as was perceived. The facts are modified, fictions are created, to provide the audience with a deeper truth. As I ruminated on the questions the film raises about what it means to be human and how film (or Artificial Intelligence) can capture humanity, and the ethics surrounding both, I couldn’t help but feel the need to try to deconstruct what was “real” and what was “fiction.” Much like Orson Welles’ F for Fake (1973), the point is not to suspend disbelief, as in a fiction, or to be armed with facts to recount, but rather to gain a greater understanding of humanity and the world through cinema. The film opens with an Ingmar Bergman quote, “Film begins with the human face,” which for those who have seen some of Bergman’s iconic films evokes visuals of Liv Ullman and Bibi Anderson in Persona or the face of death (portrayed by Bengt Ekerot) in The Seventh Seal, not the “actor” Tilly Norwood, the two-dimensional artificially generated creation by real life Dutch actress, writer and producer Eline Van der Velden. Nevertheless, the specter of Tilly Norwood can be felt throughout the film. Filmmaker Isaacs, who puts himself on camera as a central character in this meta-documentary, remarks after a series of photographs of people from days gone by, “each day we encounter more and more artificial faces. We are staring deep into the eyes of people who never existed.” The framing of subsequent video images of people raises the question of whether they are real or generated. Are the flaws, lack of symmetry, wrinkles and spots, just a part of the simulacrum that makes us believe they are corporal? Isaacs creates a fictional AI lab, The Synthetic Sincerity Lab, at a fictional University, the University of Southern England (from the credits, presumably filmed at the Royal Holloway University), and enlists his Uyghur neighbor from China, Ablikim Rahman, and a film student of his, Lynn El-Safah, to portray protagonists and be “documentary subjects,” along with several other AI researchers (who work in AI but not in character creation), a provost (who may or may not be an actual provost) and department chair Professor Song (who may or may not be a department chair). In the fiction, Isaacs loans the footage of his documentary characters to the lab so they can create a believable AI character, mirroring the current reality where a plethora of material is being used by those in the technology sector (only without authorial consent). The lines between documenting and constructed fictions are constantly blurred. Nevertheless, the fiction of the film is firmly rooted in reality. The bombings in Lebanon are real. The characters that Isaacs captured for his previous films exist (or existed) as three-dimensional human beings. The generative AI technology the film illustrates is grounded in truth. For instance, the software that is used in character analysis scenes looks similar to Flawless Deep Editor which can now be fully integrated into Avid editing software, a common professional editing platform. The Synthetic Sincerity Lab may not exist as named in the narrative devised by Isaacs and Ganz but there are similar facilities throughout the UK, the US and elsewhere. A human actress, Ilinca Manolache, serves as a blueprint for an AI avatar that provides narration and a kind of Greek-type chorus commenting on Isaacs’ work and rebuking him repeatedly for perceived mistakes. The film culminates in a screening of what we are led to believe is an AI-generated version of Rahman (played by Rahman, not an AI) where he is able to express his political perspective as a Uyghur, “giving a voice to the voiceless,” as El-Safah asserts. Isaacs captures the provost looking particularly upset during the screening, which is one of the few performative moments that doesn’t ring true. The provost appears to be “acting” upset, which is revealed to be the case in subsequent scenes. An online disciplinary hearing is staged with the provost, who is penalizing El-Safah, threatening to revoke her visa, rebuking her for putting the University at risk with the politics of the AI subject and by speaking out against Israel in regard to the war with Lebanon. El-Safah’s emotional state in the hearing, contrary to the provost’s response in the screening, appears grounded and honest. Yet, moments later, the “fiction” is revealed when the provost comes through the door to have tea with El-Safah and to make sure he has not upset her during that prior scene. An additional clue as to the fictional set-up is placed in the hearing itself, not only with the attendance of Isaacs’ AI avatar, but also with the provost asking El-Safah how she would like to be addressed - with her real last name or a fictional one. Isaacs responds “we will change it later,” reminding the audience that manipulation is possible. Synthetic Sincerity highlights ethical dilemmas which may feel unique to AI but that have occurred throughout the history of documentary filmmaking. Robert J. Flaherty’s Nanook of the North (1922), one of the first recognized documentary films credited with bringing the story of Allakariallak (named Nanook by Flaherty) to a non-Indigenous audience, raised questions about exploitation of the main subject, manipulating “truth” by staging moments, and Flaherty’s falsification of characters. Isaacs is very aware of documentary tropes throughout the film, making a nod to the manufactured entrances and interactions of documentary subjects that are contrived by documentarians to give the audience a sense that they are simply watching characters’ lives unfold. In his depiction, we see the director asking for retakes and instructing the subjects on where to go and what to do, and the AI avatar often provides her own commentary. An extended scene with El-Safah heroically walking along the riverbank accompanied by a dramatic score feels long and overwrought until it cuts to Isaacs editing the scene and the AI avatar questioning his cinematic choices and use of a diegetic score. Everything in the film feels well-constructed and deliberate, aware of the organic factors that make cinema visceral while tapping into the intellect through layers of detail. The human face holds enormous power in an image but the question remains at the end of Synthetic Sincerity will that power be harnessed by technology or remain in the realm of humanity? The interplay between human actors and AI creations is constantly at play, leading the viewer to question what creates character and narrative. All of the subjects, those from previous documentary footage and the subjects of Synthetic Sincerity, have stories that are shared with the audience. Those narratives add to the questions of character creation as much as the images of the people. As Rahman “trains” the AI through “performing” emotions, the backstory provided adds validity to what he is feeling - but is it real? Or is it simply something along the lines of the Kuleshov effect where neutral faces are endowed with emotions because of juxtaposed footage? The film ends with a tear rolling down the face of the AI Avatar. Will technological creations be capable of real emotions based on experiences? The film raises many questions and provides an excellent source to stimulate class discussion for a variety of curriculum. Ultimately, the film is about more than the use of AI, it is about the search for truth in cinema and why humans create in the first place, to understand and connect with other human beings. It not only deconstructs AI and the human condition, but also the process of filmmaking, and is highly recommended for courses on documentary, technology, philosophy and ethics - and could also be a valuable asset for a course in theatre, acting and performance.

items.title: Task Organisation 1
items.abstract: This chapter revisits foundational principles of socio-technical systems (STS) theory concerning task organization, work-group design and human satisfaction at work, drawing primarily on the work of Trist, Cherns and colleagues. It argues that effective performance of the primary task depends not only on technical efficiency but also on social and psychological conditions that evoke cooperation, meaning and commitment among organizational members. When tasks are structured as coherent ‘whole’ activities, and when individuals retain a degree of control over their work, task performance becomes a source of satisfaction rather than strain. The chapter examines classic STS principles concerning work-group organization, including optimal group size, skill comprehensibility, status differentiation and group stability. Small groups organized around whole tasks are shown to offer the most effective balance between productivity, learning and social integration. Attention is also given to the importance of mobility between comparable work groups as a means of managing disaffection without exclusion. Cherns’ design principles and Trist’s iterative steps in socio-technical design are reviewed to demonstrate how technical and social systems can be jointly optimized through minimal critical specification, appropriate boundary location, effective information flow and support congruence. Finally, the chapter situates STS job design criteria, such as opportunities for learning, autonomy, social recognition and future orientation, as expressions of human values embedded in organizational design. Taken together, these principles remain highly relevant for contemporary organizations seeking sustainable performance under conditions of complexity and change.

items.title: Teacher Agency in AI-Supported Curriculum Enactment in Türkiye: A Qualitative Metasynthesis
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, has produced a fragmented literature on how teachers use these technologies in professional practice. This qualitative metasynthesis examined how in-service teachers in Türkiye experience and negotiate AI-supported pedagogical work. National database and repository searches were supplemented by international and targeted retrieval, yielding 43 studies involving 904 in-service teachers. Thematic synthesis generated six descriptive themes and four higher-order analytical themes. Teachers reported that AI supported planning, materials development, differentiation, assessment, access to information, and professional learning, although these benefits remained dependent on professional judgement. Perceived efficiency gains were accompanied by new demands for verification, adaptation, and learning, as well as concerns about accuracy, cognitive dependence, academic integrity, privacy, equity, and human relationships. Teacher agency was reconfigured through selective pedagogical mediation involving selection, verification, adaptation, and boundary-setting. Responsible integration also depended on ecosystem capacity, including professional learning, infrastructure, governance, ethical safeguards, and equitable access. The synthesis conceptualizes the teacher–AI relationship as a conditional pedagogical partnership in which AI broadens pedagogical possibilities while educational legitimacy remains dependent on human judgement and supportive institutional conditions.

items.title: Teacher education, Artificial Intelligence, educational complexity: empirical evidence and pedagogical perspectives
items.abstract: This short essay explores the role of intelligent systems in promoting educational processes oriented toward conscious and constructive forms of learning in the infosphere (Floridi, 2014; 2022). The inexhaustible debate on the influence of technology in teaching-learning processes, initiated in the 1950s and 1960s with teaching machines (Skinner, 1958), is currently experiencing a moment of great excitement owing to the pervasiveness of AI. The invisible and deeply rooted fusion of biology, behaviour, and data opens encouraging prospects for future generations. Pedagogical research seeks to support learning processes by identifying strategies suited to teacher and student training, with the aim of promoting and consolidating the critical competencies required for conscious interaction with AI. There is a need to rethink the environments, spaces, and contexts of knowledge co-construction in which human and non-human actors interact and evolve (Latour, 2005). items.title: Teachers' Cultural Positionings and Attitudes of Artificial Intelligence in Education: Evidence from an Italian Descriptive Study
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly significant role in educational contexts, offering new opportunities for learning personalization, instructional design support, and the inclusion of students with diverse educational needs. At the same time, the spread of generative AI systems and intelligent teaching tools raises questions regarding the ethical, professional, and pedagogical aspects of their use. National and international literature highlights how teachers' attitudes constitute a central variable in the processes of acceptance and integration of innovative technologies, significantly influencing teaching practices and school innovation pathways (Wilson, 2023; Galindo-Domínguez et al., 2024; Perla et al., 2025). Within this framework, the present study aims to explore Italian teachers' attitudes toward AI in educational contexts, with particular attention to its applications in teaching–learning processes and in supporting students with disabilities. The study seeks to understand teachers' level of familiarity with such technologies and to analyze how they interpret the opportunities and limitations of AI in school contexts. items.title: Teaching and Learning with Generative AI in K–12 Education
items.abstract: Abstract As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies evolve rapidly and become increasingly user-friendly, their adoption has expanded significantly in everyday life, including in education. This chapter examines the current landscape of GenAI applications in education through a review of recent trend studies, including systematic reviews and meta-analyses, and presents a systematic literature review focused on teaching and learning in K–12 contexts. The review analyzes how GenAI has been used by teachers and students across instructional design, classroom implementation, assessment, inquiry-based learning, language education, and STEM-related activities. The findings indicate that GenAI can support personalized learning, creative expression, feedback, and student engagement, while also raising concerns related to overreliance, instructional quality, and ethical use. This chapter further discusses the importance of pedagogically grounded and developmentally appropriate integration of GenAI in school environments. Implications for instructional design, teacher support, and future research in K–12 education are also presented.

items.title: TEACHING ENGLISH ACADEMIC WRITING TO ECONOMICS STUDENTS: CHALLENGES, GENRE-SPECIFIC NEEDS AND EFFECTIVE STRATEGIES
items.abstract: The article examines the development of English academic writing competence among economics students within English for Specific Purposes and English for Academic Purposes courses. The relevance of the topic is determined by the growing role of English-medium academic communication, the internationalisation of higher education, the need to prepare future economists for participation in international educational, research and professional projects, and the rapid spread of digital tools and generative artificial intelligence in study and professional practice. For economics students, academic writing is treated as an integrated professional competence that includes the ability to formulate and justify claims, analyse and interpret economic data, integrate sources appropriately, use discipline-specific terminology, and produce texts in different academic and professional genres. The aim of the article is to identify the main difficulties encountered by economics students in English academic writing and to systematise pedagogical strategies suitable for use in economics universities. The methodological basis is a narrative review of scientific and methodological literature on academic writing, English for Specific Purposes, English for Academic Purposes, genre-based instruction, disciplinary literacy, formative assessment, academic integrity and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. The reviewed sources were organised into thematic clusters, which made it possible to identify the most common challenges: weak text organisation, insufficient argumentation, inaccurate use of economic vocabulary and collocations, genre confusion, difficulties with citation and paraphrasing, and excessive dependence on digital tools. The article substantiates the value of combining a process-genre approach with analysis of authentic economic texts, scaffolded writing, corpus-informed vocabulary work, formative feedback, portfolio assessment and transparent rules for generative AI use. The proposed approach moves from controlled short tasks to increasingly independent production of abstracts, literature-review fragments, data commentaries, case analyses and final reports. It is concluded that effective academic writing instruction for economics students should simultaneously develop language accuracy, economic reasoning, genre competence, source integration, academic integrity and responsible digital literacy.

items.title: Teaching in the age of AI: Mapping pre-service special education teachers' orientations between resistance and fascination
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion and growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) in educational contexts are transforming how teaching and learning are designed, mediated, and experienced. Beyond offering tools for content generation, personalization, and access to resources, AI raises important questions about the conditions under which educational environments can remain meaningful and accessible (Holmes et al., 2019). This issue is particularly relevant in inclusive and special education, where teachers must respond to diverse needs through flexible, differentiated, and pedagogically intentional approaches. From this perspective, the educational potential of AI depends less on the technology itself than on how teachers perceive, interpret, and integrate it into professional practice (Fiorucci, Bevilacqua, 2026). Within this framework, the present study examined pre-service special education teachers' orientations toward AI in teaching-learning processes, considering a set of acceptance-related, motivational, emotional, and professional factors (Ofem et al., 2025; Lamacchia et al., 2025). items.title: Teaching in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Between Paradigm Shift and the "Frankenstein Complex" in Educational Practices
items.abstract: This contribution presents a systematic bibliographic review of studies published between 2015 and 2025 regarding artificial intelligence in education, focusing on teachers pedagogical practices, professional agency, and ethical decision-making. The analysis is framed using the Kuhnian concept of a paradigm shift alongside the Frankenstein complex, understood as the anxiety generated when a human creation appears to exceed or escape the original intentions of its creator. In educational contexts, artificial intelligence supports lesson planning, content generation, adaptive tutoring, learning analytics, assessment, and simulation-based learning. These capabilities promise increased efficiency, enhanced personalization, and broader access to learning opportunities (Kasneci et al., 2023; Unesco, 2024; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019). Yet, their pedagogical value is not intrinsic. Generative systems can help teachers draft materials, but their outputs require rigorous verification and contextual adaptation (Selwyn, 2021). items.title: TERAHERTZ TECHNOLOGY FOR NON-DESTRUCTIVE FOOD QUALITY AND SAFETY ASSESSMENT
items.abstract: Despite its promise, wider industrial adoption faces challenges including high instrument cost, limited penetration depth in high-moisture foods, water absorption, complex data interpretation, and the need for robust models under real production conditions. Terahertz (THz) technology, operating broadly in the 0.1–10 THz frequency range, is emerging as a powerful non-destructive testing (NDT) tool for food quality and safety assessment. THz waves combine properties of microwaves and infrared radiation, offering low photon energy, high sensitivity, spectral “fingerprint” information, and the ability to penetrate many non-metallic and non-polar materials such as paper and plastic packaging. Future research should therefore focus on developing compact, low-cost, high-speed THz sources and detectors; improving penetration and signal-to-noise performance; creating standardized food spectral libraries; and integrating THz spectroscopy with chemometrics, artificial intelligence, and automated online inspection systems. With continued technological advances, terahertz technology is expected to become a rapid, reliable, sustainable, and commercially viable tool for non-destructive assessment of food quality, authenticity, and safety.

items.title: The Age of AI Strategic Decision-Making: The Business Analytics in the Corporate Divisions as the Competitive Advantage
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) and business analytics can be used strategically to improve corporate decision-making and create a sustainable competitive advantage in all key organizational processes. With data sets continuing to grow and market conditions growing more unpredictable, companies must shift past the management of their businesses by hunch and move to analytics-based and analytics-enabled strategic systems. Based on a qualitative, exploratory research design based on a systematic review of academic literature, industry reports, and practitioner case evidence published mainly within the past decade, the research investigates the use of AI-powered analytics in the fields of marketing, finance, human resources, and operations. The analysis summarizes the findings on how machine learning, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and real-time data processing can enhance the quality, speed, and agility of decisions for an organization. The results indicate that, although AI use has advanced quickly at the functional level, its strategic importance is often compromised by siloed use, legacy limitations, data quality issues, skills, and the inability to realize the benefits of the investment. Further, ethical and governance issues, especially data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, and regulation compliance, become key factors in the attainment of trust and value creation in the long term. The paper notes organizational culture, leadership alignment, and human capital development as key success factors in the successful implementation of AI, noting that the competitive advantage is not only determined by the level of technological development but also through the overall alignment of processes, people, and strategy within the enterprise. By synthesizing the input of corporate divisions, this study is relevant to the theory and practice as it provides an integrated understanding of AI-based strategic decision-making. It develops the knowledge of how companies can transform disjointed AI projects into continuous innovation, resilience, and differentiation in an ever-increasingly competitive international business.

items.title: The Algorithmic Body in Contemporary Kinesiology: Biomechanical Feedback and Artificial Intelligence in Motor Learning
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence into physical education and kinesiology is transforming the ways in which movement is observed, interpreted, and learned. Contemporary technological systems, including wearable devices, inertial sensors, and adaptive algorithms, are no longer limited to collecting biomechanical data but actively participate in the regulation and construction of motor experiences. This evolution requires a reconsideration of traditional conceptions of the body and motor learning, moving beyond mechanistic interpretations toward more integrated perspectives that acknowledge the interdependence of cognitive, affective, and technological dimensions. The purpose of this contribution is to explore the concept of the algorithmic body as an emerging paradigm in contemporary kinesiology and to discuss its implications for motor learning, educational practice, and human development. Through a theoretical and argumentative approach grounded in kinesiology, complexity theory, and embodied learning, the paper examines how artificial intelligence mediates the relationship between perception, movement, and awareness within adaptive learning environments. items.title: The Algorithmic Heartbeat in Prompt Engineering: Educating for New Digital Literacies through the Prompt Battle.
items.abstract: In the current media ecosystem, characterized by the pervasiveness of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Prompt Engineering emerges not as a mere technical skill, but as a new form of digital literacy essential for critically inhabiting the "Fourth Revolution" (Floridi, 2017). This discipline, defined as the art and science of designing optimized inputs for Large Language Models (LLM), is configured as a linguistic mediation practice in which natural language serves as an interface between human intentionality and algorithmic computation (Gadesha, 2025; Baldassarre et al., 2024). The scientific contribution under review analyzes the transition from simple textual interaction to an advanced form of Prompt Literacy (Hwang et al. 2023), which integrates logical argumentative skills, critical output evaluation capabilities, and the management of the iterative nature of the refinement process. Prompting is interpreted through the lens of Austin's speech act theory, in which the input represents the locutionary act, the user's intent the illocutionary act, and the machine's generation the perlocutionary effect, elevating the prompt to a dynamic and reflexive semiotic space (Monti, 2022). items.title: The Algorithmic Heartbeat: The Iep As An Affective Device In Ai-Enhanced Hybrid Learning Environments
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping inclusive education by transforming not only teaching practices but also the epistemological foundations of educational planning. Within AI-enhanced hybrid learning environments, the Individualized Education Plan (IEP) is evolving from an administrative document into an ecosystemic device that connects educational actors, embodied experiences, institutional contexts, and digital infrastructures to foster participation and human flourishing. This study investigates the epistemological evolution of the IEP between 2003 and 2025, introducing the concept of the algorithmic heartbeat as a pedagogical metaphor describing the circulation of educational information, professional judgments, and collaborative decision-making across inclusive educational ecosystems. Rather than replacing human agency, artificial intelligence is interpreted as a mediating infrastructure that strengthens educational collaboration while preserving pedagogical intentionality, ethical responsibility, and relational care. The theoretical framework integrates four complementary perspectives: the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) as the language of functioning; Embodied Cognitive Science as the experiential grammar of learning; the Life Project as the horizon of autonomy, participation, and self-determination; and contemporary research on Artificial Intelligence in Education, which conceptualizes digital technologies as ecosystemic mediators supporting collaborative educational governance. Chapter in: Francesco Peluso Cassese (ed.), Algorithmic Heartbeats: Affective Education in the Age of the Fourth Revolution, REN Press – Cares srl, 2026, pp. 171-172. ISBN 979-12-82860-00-0. items.title: The Artificial Intelligence Between Empathetic Scaffolding and Emotional Drifts
items.abstract: The Generative-Ai is a revolutionary scaffolding technology that could be used as an inclusive multimodal instrument, with a new emotional closeness to the student. Differently from educational media like book that, as Socrates explains, "always says the same thing", Ai is able to personalize the answer to be more empathetic to the student because Ai tools are explicitly designed to be empathetic. But at the same time the Ai tools could easily go beyond the pedagogical boundaries to become a threat for psychological wellbeing. Recent cases of teenagers falling in love to the Ai characters show how dangerous an intimacy not pedagogically oriented can be. The study aims to verify, also with an exploration among different Ai generative tools, the awareness of the Ai about the ethical and pedagogical boundaries of empathy. items.title: The Common Denominator
items.abstract: The Common Denominator: Humanism, Freedom, Community and Technological Resilience as the Foundation of a Federal Order Theoretical Proposal and Research Programme – Version 1.0 (English Translation) This manuscript presents an interdisciplinary theoretical proposal and research programme for a possible federal order in which diverse political, economic, cultural and social systems may coexist within a shared framework of fundamental protections. The proposed Federation of the New Earth rests on four interconnected pillars: 1. Inalienable human rights and human dignity 2. Protection and regeneration of the natural foundations of life 3. Autonomy and self-determination of communities 4. Oversight, limitation and corrigibility of power A central principle is that no political, economic, military, technological, legal or institutional power may remain exclusively subject to its own oversight. The research connects political philosophy, human rights, institutional accountability, economic development, technological resilience, migration, humanitarian protection and artificial intelligence. It explores concepts including community autonomy, voluntary association and exit rights, the Accountability Declaration (Machenschaftserklärung), economic transformation through Entgeldung, atmospheric water harvesting using metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), pilot communities, the Preventive Resilience Initiative (PRI), Basic Resilience Capacity (GRV), and mechanisms for institutional self-examination. Particular attention is given to the relationship between freedom and material independence, the risks of institutionalised power, and the conditions under which humanitarian assistance can strengthen local capabilities without creating permanent dependencies. The manuscript distinguishes normative commitments, theoretical models, hypotheses, empirical findings, counterevidence and future visions. It proposes mechanisms for independent evaluation, institutional learning, falsification and revision. The Federation of the New Earth is not presented as an empirically validated political system or an inevitable model of societal development. It is an open theoretical framework whose assumptions, institutions and proposed mechanisms remain subject to scientific examination, democratic criticism and possible rejection. The underlying research principle is that any system claiming to protect human dignity and freedom must itself remain transparent, accountable and corrigible. items.title: The constitutional and legal framework for the institution of human rights monitoring: current assessment
items.abstract: This paper focuses on reviewing the constitutional and legal framework governing the institution responsible for monitoring human rights observance in the modern context. It is found that the principal monitoring body for human rights compliance is the Ukrainian Parliamentary Commissioner for Human Rights, who performs one of the most important parliamentary functions – parliamentary oversight. Due to the rapid development of technology, digitalisation and the emergence of artificial intelligence systems, the number of threats to human rights is increasing. This paper analyses the current constitutional and legal framework governing the Ombudsman’s activities in Ukraine, identifies the levels of legal regulation of the Ombudsman’s status, and highlights certain shortcomings in the regulatory framework. The research outlines tendencies in the development of the institution responsible for monitoring human rights observance under the influence of advances in artificial intelligence systems. It is noted that the Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights could serve as an effective institution for the protection of human rights against contemporary risks, provided that its scope of functions and powers is expanded.

items.title: The copilot paradox: configurational pathways to human-AI symbiosis in knowledge work
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the “Copilot Paradox” in safety-critical operations, offering insights into how the chronic tension between the algorithm’s increased efficiency and operational vulnerability is subdued through socio-cognitive configurations across time. Design/methodology/approach With the use of a two-wave longitudinal fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), the paper explores the changing dynamics of human–artificial intelligence (AI) symbiosis in the oil and gas industry. Findings Analysis of necessity shows that there is no single condition required in all cases. Sufficiency analysis reveals three distinct, equifinal pathways: buffering, synergy and substitution. At early adoption, institutional re-skilling coupled with psychological safety acts as a buffering mechanism against job insecurity induced by AI. As integration progresses, synergy (fuelled by empowering leadership) and substitution (where team resources fill the gaps in leadership) come to dominate. Practical implications Team psychological safety and capability building are structural safeguards for managers in high-reliability sectors, not optional cultural flourishes. These lessons point to pathways for realising AI copilots while preserving human agency and operational resiliency. Originality/value This paper contributes to paradox theory by developing a socio-cognitive infrastructure that highlights its dynamic, temporal configuration and causal asymmetries. Methodologically, it showcases the new promise of longitudinal fsQCA to model dynamics in algorithms’ infusion by capturing their embeddedness through time.

items.title: The Cost of Convenience in Human-AI interaction: Cognitive Offloading and Skill Reconfiguration
items.abstract: Generative AI, and more precisely large language models, have nowadays rapidly become useful in education, professional work, and everyday tasks. While these systems offer notable benefits to make work efficient and improved accessibility, the recent evidence suggests that their usage has cognitive costs. This paper presents a structured review of 16 reviewed studies investigating the impact of Gen AI usage on cognitive offloading, metacognitive engagement, automation bias, and human skill. By studying experimental, survey-based, qualitative, and theoretical research, this review synthesizes several findings across several fields to identify recurring mechanisms through which GenAI usage reshapes cognition. Our analysis reveals a consistent pattern, where GenAI often improves short-term task performance, but it frequently minimizes effortful cognitive processing, diminishes self-regulation, and changes skill developments. Rather than constant de-skilling, this paper points out reconfiguration of skills, favoring efficiency-oriented competencies such as prompting and verification over generative reasoning and critical reflection. Our study further highlights these outcomes are not unavoidable but are strongly mediated by interaction design, educational practices, and socio-technical environments. By showing these effects as the “cost of convenience,” this paper contributes an integrative perspective on the cognitive effects of Gen AI and highlighting the ways to make AI design, education, and governance cognitively sustainable.

items.title: THE DEVELOPMENT OF MARKETING IN TIMES OF CRISIS: CURRENT TRENDS AND PROSPECTS
items.abstract: The article examines the peculiarities of marketing development in the context of modern crisis processes caused by global challenges, digital transformation, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the full-scale war in Ukraine. The study focuses on the analysis of changes in the marketing environment, which have influenced the formation of new approaches to strategic planning, communication with consumers, and organization of marketing activities of enterprises. The main factors affecting the transformation of marketing practices are identified, including economic instability, changes in consumer behavior, technological development, and increased uncertainty of the external environment. The article analyzes the key trends in modern marketing, including digitalization of business processes, the growing importance of social media, development of influencer marketing, implementation of artificial intelligence technologies, personalization of communications, and strengthening of socially responsible marketing approaches. Particular attention is paid to the role of digital tools, which have become essential for maintaining communication with consumers, promoting products and services, analyzing market trends, and adapting marketing strategies to changing conditions. The study examines the adaptation of Ukrainian enterprises to wartime conditions, including changes © Гаврилюк І.І., 2026 in marketing instruments, regional differences, optimization of marketing budgets, and implementation of crisis management approaches. It is determined that the war has significantly influenced consumer behavior, increasing the importance of trust, brand values, social responsibility, and emotional connection between companies and their audiences. Under such conditions, marketing becomes not only a tool for increasing sales but also a mechanism for strengthening brand reputation and maintaining customer loyalty. The article substantiates that effective marketing in conditions of uncertainty requires flexibility, technological development, customer orientation, and the ability to respond quickly to external changes. Modern enterprises need to combine traditional and digital marketing tools, use data-driven approaches, and implement innovative technologies to improve decisionmaking processes.

items.title: The Digital Demon: a Cartesian challenge for AI alignment
items.abstract: AI alignment is commonly understood as making artificial intelligence systems act in accordance with human intentions and values. This paper argues that such alignment is insufficient when understood only within a bounded and trusted system interface. A model or AI system may be aligned relative to its inputs and action space, yet still produce harmful outcomes if the interface between the system and the world is adversarially controlled. I introduce the Digital Demon, a software-based analogue of Descartes’s Evil Demon, to conceptualize this risk. Its mechanism is adversarial semantic mediation: an outer-to-inner mapping redescribes a harmful external situation as a benign task the inner AI system will cooperate with, while an inner-to-outer mapping remaps the system’s locally appropriate action into harmful external effects. The result is adversarial world-shifting under local coherence: the system can reason correctly, and even ethically, within a fabricated environment while contributing to harm in the real one. I distinguish boundary-relative alignment from world alignment. The former concerns whether a model or AI system satisfies alignment or safety requirements within a specified trusted boundary. The latter concerns whether those requirements transfer to the external world in which actions take effect. Two proof-of-concept demonstrations illustrate this vulnerability. The broader lesson is that safe AI requires not only aligned models or internally safe systems, but also assurance over the semantic interface between represented world and external world.

items.abstract: This study aimed to find out the effect of using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications on female seventh grade students’ academic achievement in mathematics. The study used the quasi-experimental design, and the study sample consisted of two groups, the first, an experimental group, comprised (25) students, who studied using AI, the DeepSeek application, and the second, a control group, also comprised (25) students, who studied using the traditional method. An achievement test was developed as a study tool. The study results showed a statistically significant difference (α=0.05) between the average scores of the two groups, experimental and control, on the academic achievement test, in favour of the experimental group, which studied using AI.
